title: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning
scopeHtml: Scope: LoRA, QLoRA, full fine-tuning, hyperparameters, evaluation and deployment.

notes.title: Full fine-tuning vs parameter-efficient
notes.html:
Full fine-tuning (FFT). Update all weights with gradient descent on your data.

  • Memory: weights + gradients + optimizer states. With AdamW in mixed precision it's roughly 16 bytes per parameter (2 weights bf16 + 2 grads + 4 master weights fp32 + 8 for Adam moments): a 7B model needs ~110 GB, a 70B model >1 TB before sharding/activations. Techniques: ZeRO/FSDP sharding, gradient checkpointing, 8-bit optimizers.
  • Pros: highest capacity to adapt, best for large distribution shifts or continued pretraining.
  • Cons: costly, risk of catastrophic forgetting, one full model copy per task (storage and serving), harder to roll back.

Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT). Freeze base weights; train a small number of extra parameters (0.01 to 2% of the model). Benefits: far less memory (no optimizer state for the frozen base), small artifacts (MBs), multiple tasks sharing one base, easy rollback, less forgetting. Cost: slightly lower ceiling on some hard tasks (often negligible).

Families. LoRA/QLoRA (low-rank adapters), (IA)³, prefix/prompt tuning, adapters (bottleneck layers), BitFit (bias only), DoRA and LoRA variants.

Choosing. Start with LoRA/QLoRA; move to full fine-tuning only if evals show a quality gap that more rank/targets can't close and you have the compute.

Real life. Repainting a whole house versus hanging a few new pictures and swapping them when needed.

notes.title: LoRA
notes.html:
Idea. For a weight matrix W (d × k), learn a low-rank update ΔW = B·A with A (r × k), B (d × r), r ≪ min(d, k). Forward: y = Wx + (α/r)·B(Ax). Only A and B are trained; A is initialized randomly, B to zero so training starts from the base model. Trainable parameters per matrix: r(d + k) instead of d·k.

Example. d = k = 4096, r = 16: 131k parameters vs 16.8M (0.8%). Applied to all attention (and MLP) projections of a 7B model: ~20 to 80 M trainable parameters.

Hyperparameters.

  • Rank r (8, 16, 64): capacity; higher for complex tasks; diminishing returns.
  • Alpha α: scaling (commonly α = r or 2r); effective step size.
  • Target modules: attention q,k,v,o and often MLP gate/up/down; more targets = more capacity.
  • Dropout (0 to 0.1) to regularize.
  • Learning rate: higher than full fine-tuning (1e-4 to 3e-4), cosine/linear decay with warmup.
  • Batch size/epochs: 1 to 3 epochs for most instruction datasets.

Serving.

  • Merge the adapter into the base weights (W' = W + BA) for zero inference overhead, but you lose swap-ability.
  • Dynamic adapters: keep the base loaded and apply adapters per request (multi-LoRA serving: S-LoRA, vLLM LoRA) — efficient multi-tenant customization.

Code sketch.

from peft import LoraConfig, get_peft_model
cfg = LoraConfig(r=16, lora_alpha=32, lora_dropout=0.05,
                 target_modules=["q_proj","k_proj","v_proj","o_proj","gate_proj","up_proj","down_proj"],
                 task_type="CAUSAL_LM")
model = get_peft_model(base_model, cfg)   # base frozen, adapters trainable

Real life. A removable overlay on a map instead of redrawing the map.

notes.title: QLoRA
notes.html:
Idea. Quantize the frozen base model to 4-bit (NormalFloat4, NF4) with double quantization, keep LoRA adapters in bf16, backprop through the dequantized weights, and use paged optimizers to handle memory spikes. Result: fine-tune a 65 to 70B model on a single 48 to 80 GB GPU, or a 7 to 13B model on a consumer GPU, with quality close to 16-bit LoRA.

Memory arithmetic. 70B in NF4 ≈ 35 to 40 GB for weights, plus activations/adapters/optimizer for the LoRA params (tiny), so ~48 GB total with gradient checkpointing vs >1 TB for full fine-tuning.

Trade-offs. Slower than bf16 LoRA (dequantization overhead, ~20 to 40%); small quality loss; the quantized base affects the final merged model, so merge into a 16-bit copy or re-quantize carefully and re-evaluate.

Real life. Working from a compressed copy of the textbook while writing your notes in full resolution.

notes.title: Training practices
notes.html:
Setup checklist.

  1. Choose the base model (instruct vs base, size, licence, tokenizer, context length).
  2. Format data with the exact chat template; mask loss on prompt tokens (train on assistant tokens).
  3. Pack or bucket sequences by length for efficiency; handle max length without truncating answers.
  4. Hyperparameters: LoRA lr ~2e-4 (full FT ~1e-5), warmup 3 to 10%, cosine decay, weight decay 0 to 0.1, batch size 16 to 128 effective, 1 to 3 epochs.
  5. Precision: bf16 mixed precision; gradient checkpointing for memory; FlashAttention.
  6. Monitor: training loss, validation loss every N steps, sample generations, grad norm, learning rate; log to W&B/MLflow.
  7. Early stopping/checkpoint selection by validation loss and task eval (loss isn't the metric you care about).

Diagnosing curves. Train loss falling, validation loss rising = overfitting (reduce epochs/rank, more data, regularize). Both flat = too low LR/too little capacity/bad data. Spikes = LR too high, bad batches. Training loss near zero quickly = memorization or leakage.

Catastrophic forgetting. Narrow fine-tuning degrades general abilities. Mitigate: LoRA/low rank, low LR, fewer epochs, mix general instruction data (5 to 30%) into the training set, replay data, regularization (e.g. KL to base), evaluate on general benchmarks and safety probes.

Reproducibility. Fix seeds, record data/config/code versions, store checkpoints and the evaluation reports.

Real life. Coaching an athlete: enough training to improve, not so much that they're injured or forget other skills.

notes.title: Evaluating and deploying
notes.html:
Evaluation.

  • Task metrics on the held-out test set vs baselines (prompted base, stronger model).
  • Behavioural checks: format validity rates, refusal behaviour, tool-calling accuracy, long-input handling.
  • Regression suite: general benchmarks and in-house probes.
  • Safety: red-team prompts; fine-tuning can erode safety behaviour, so re-test.
  • Human review of samples; LLM judge calibrated.
  • Cost/latency: tokens saved, throughput on target hardware.

Deployment options.

  • Hosted fine-tuning APIs (simple; limited model choice/control; data leaves your environment; check retention terms).
  • Self-hosted: vLLM/TGI/TensorRT-LLM serving the merged model or multi-LoRA.
  • Quantize for serving (AWQ/GPTQ/FP8) and re-evaluate.

Operations. Version datasets, configs, adapters and evaluation reports together; canary rollout with the base model as fallback; monitor drift (new topics, formats); retraining triggers (new data volume, metric decay, requirement changes); retention and deletion of training data (privacy).

Real life. Road-testing a tuned car before it goes on sale, then watching warranty claims.

notes.title: Alternatives and related methods
notes.html:
• Prompt/prefix tuning: learn soft prompt vectors; very light but usually weaker than LoRA.
  • Adapters (bottleneck layers): add small modules; add inference latency unless fused.
  • Continued pretraining: further next-token training on domain text (legal, biomedical, code) to absorb vocabulary and style before SFT; expensive, needs lots of text.
  • Preference optimization (DPO, KTO, ORPO) to shape quality and safety after SFT.
  • Distillation: train a small student from a strong teacher's outputs (see optimization notes).
  • Model merging (weight averaging, TIES, DARE) to combine skills without training; experimental, evaluate carefully.
  • Embedding/reranker fine-tuning for retrieval with (query, positive, hard negative) triples.
  • Hosted vs open weights: hosted is convenient; open weights give control and portability.

Choosing. Start with the lightest approach that clears the eval: prompt → LoRA SFT → add preference tuning if needed → full fine-tune/continued pretraining only with strong evidence.

Real life. Choosing between a tailored suit, alterations, and off-the-peg.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
FFT vs PEFT. Full fine-tuning updates everything (~16 bytes/param with AdamW, risk of forgetting, one model per task). PEFT freezes the base and trains tiny modules; LoRA is the default.

LoRA. ΔW = BA with rank r; trainable ≈ r(d+k) per matrix; hyperparameters rank, alpha, target modules, dropout, LR ~1e-4 to 3e-4; merge for zero overhead or serve multi-LoRA adapters per tenant. QLoRA adds 4-bit NF4 base + paged optimizers, enabling 70B fine-tuning on one big GPU at slight speed/quality cost.

Training. Exact chat template, loss on assistant tokens only, 1 to 3 epochs, warmup + decay, monitor validation loss and real task metrics, early stop; mitigate forgetting with low rank/LR and general-data replay; fix seeds and version everything.

Evaluation and deployment. Compare to prompted baselines; check regressions, safety, format validity, cost/latency; hosted API vs self-hosted; quantize and re-test; canary with fallback; retraining triggers; privacy for training data.

Alternatives. Prompt tuning, adapters, continued pretraining, DPO/KTO/ORPO, distillation, model merging, retriever fine-tuning.

Interview one-liners.

  • "LoRA trains a low-rank delta; merge it for free inference or keep it swappable."
  • "QLoRA = 4-bit frozen base + bf16 adapters."
  • "Validation loss is not your metric; run the task eval."
  • "Fine-tuning can erode safety and general skills: test for regressions."

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between full fine-tuning and parameter-efficient fine-tuning, and why has PEFT become the default?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks that you know fine-tuning is not one thing and can justify the cheap option with real costs.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Fine-tuning means continuing to train a pretrained model on my own examples so it behaves the way I want. Full fine-tuning updates every weight, so it needs memory for weights, gradients and optimizer state and produces a full model copy per task. PEFT freezes the base model and trains a tiny set of extra parameters (often under 2% of the model), so it is far cheaper, the artifact is megabytes, and one base model can serve many tasks. I start with PEFT, usually LoRA, and only go to full fine-tuning if evals show a gap that more adapter capacity cannot close.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A "weight" is one learned number in the network. A 7B model has 7 billion of them. Training = nudging weights using gradients computed on examples.

Full FT : all 7B weights trainable -> grads for 7B + optimizer state for 7B
PEFT    : 7B weights frozen        -> grads/optimizer only for ~40M extra weights

Why PEFT wins by default: (1) no gradients or optimizer state for the frozen base, which is the dominant memory cost; (2) the output is a small adapter file you can version, swap and roll back; (3) less forgetting because the base is untouched; (4) many tenants/tasks share one loaded base. The cost is a slightly lower ceiling on hard distribution shifts (new language, new domain vocabulary), where full fine-tuning or continued pretraining may be needed.

Families: LoRA/QLoRA (low-rank adapters), bottleneck adapters, prompt/prefix tuning, (IA)3, BitFit (train only biases), DoRA and other LoRA variants.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Training code is Python only (the training stack, PEFT, Transformers and PyTorch, has no Kotlin/Java equivalent); Kotlin/Java appear only when calling or serving the tuned model, see later questions.

from peft import LoraConfig, get_peft_model
model = get_peft_model(base_model, LoraConfig(r=16, lora_alpha=32, task_type="CAUSAL_LM"))
model.print_trainable_parameters()   # e.g. trainable ~0.5% of total

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying PEFT "is just smaller so it is worse". On most instruction-style tasks quality is close to full fine-tuning.
  • Forgetting that the frozen base still needs full memory for its weights (and activations).
  • Treating PEFT as a way to teach lots of new knowledge; it mainly shapes behavior.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. When is full fine-tuning justified? → Large domain shift, continued pretraining, and evals showing a gap that higher rank and more target modules did not close, plus the compute to do it.
  2. Do you still need a GPU for PEFT? → Yes; it cuts memory, not the need for the base forward/backward pass.
  3. How do you roll back a bad PEFT release? → Point serving back at the previous adapter or the base model; nothing was overwritten.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "PEFT trains fewer parameters so it is cheaper." Senior: quantifies memory per parameter, names versioning, swap and forgetting benefits, and states the evidence needed to justify escalating to full fine-tuning.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team stored a 14 GB full copy per customer; moving to 80 MB adapters on one shared base cut storage and deploy time to minutes.

questions.promptHtml: Explain LoRA. What is actually trained, and why is it called low-rank?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: LoRA is the most common PEFT method; interviewers want to see the mechanism, not the library call.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A weight matrix W is big, say 4096 by 4096. Instead of changing W, LoRA learns a small correction delta-W written as the product of two thin matrices, B (d by r) and A (r by k), where the rank r is tiny, like 16. The layer computes the frozen Wx plus a scaled B(Ax). Only A and B train. "Low-rank" means the correction is forced to live in a small r-dimensional space, which cuts trainable parameters from d times k to r times (d + k).

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Rank is the number of independent directions a matrix can act in. A full 4096x4096 matrix can act in up to 4096 directions; a product of a 4096x16 and a 16x4096 matrix can act in at most 16. The bet behind LoRA is that fine-tuning changes live in a low-dimensional subspace, so a small-rank update is enough.

Forward pass: y = W x + (alpha / r) * B (A x).

  • A starts random (Gaussian), B starts at zero, so delta-W = 0 at step 0 and the model begins exactly as the base model.
  • Parameter count for d = k = 4096, r = 16: 16 * (4096 + 4096) = 131,072 vs 16,777,216, about 0.8%.
  • Applied across all attention and MLP projections of a 7B model this gives roughly 20 to 80 M trainable parameters depending on r.
x --> [ W (frozen) ] ----------------+--> y
  \-> [ A (r x k) ] -> [ B (d x r) ] -*(alpha/r)

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Training is Python only.

from peft import LoraConfig
cfg = LoraConfig(r=16, lora_alpha=32, lora_dropout=0.05,
                 target_modules=["q_proj","k_proj","v_proj","o_proj"],
                 task_type="CAUSAL_LM")

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying LoRA compresses the model. It adds a trainable delta; the base is unchanged.
  • Confusing "rank" with "number of layers".
  • Assuming LoRA adds inference latency; it does not once merged.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why initialize B to zero? → So the starting model equals the base; random B would perturb outputs at step 0 and destabilize early training.
  2. Which matrices get adapters? → Usually attention q,k,v,o and often MLP gate/up/down.
  3. Trainable parameter count for r=8, d=k=4096? → 8 * 8192 = 65,536 per matrix.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "two small matrices instead of the big one." Senior: gives the forward formula, init reasoning, parameter arithmetic, and mentions merging and the low-intrinsic-rank hypothesis as an assumption that can fail.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An engineer set r=256 "to be safe" and lost most of the memory savings; rank is a cost knob, not a free safety margin.

questions.promptHtml: A product owner says "let's fine-tune the model on our docs so it knows our product". Is that the right approach?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The most common real-world mistake is fine-tuning for knowledge when retrieval or prompting would do.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Usually not as a first step. Fine-tuning is good at changing behavior: tone, output format, task skill, following a house style or a tool schema. It is poor and expensive for injecting fresh, changing facts, which are better served by retrieval (RAG) because you can update documents instantly and cite sources. My ladder is prompt, then RAG for knowledge, then LoRA SFT for behavior, then preference tuning, and full fine-tuning or continued pretraining only with strong evidence.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Knowledge that changes weekly (pricing, policies): retrieval. A fine-tuned model goes stale and can confidently state old facts; there is no citation.
  • Consistent JSON schema, brand voice, classification label set, domain jargon handling, small model replacing a big one for cost: fine-tuning.
  • Many good systems combine both: a LoRA-tuned model that is good at using retrieved context in the required format.
  • Decision signals: have a measured baseline with the best prompt; have at least hundreds of high-quality examples; the failure is stable and behavioral; the latency/cost target needs a smaller model.

sections.label: Code
sections.html: Training is Python only; no code needed for this decision question.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Fine-tuning before building any eval, so you cannot tell whether it helped.
  • Expecting the model to memorize a document set reliably from a few epochs.
  • Ignoring that training data may contain personal data that must later be deleted.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How many examples do you need? → Hundreds to a few thousand clean ones often suffice for behavior; quality beats quantity.
  2. Can fine-tuning reduce hallucination? → It can teach abstaining and format discipline, but it does not add verified knowledge.
  3. How do you combine with RAG? → Train on examples that include retrieved context so the model learns to ground answers in it.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "fine-tune so it learns our data." Senior: separates knowledge from behavior, proposes the ladder, and insists on a baseline eval first.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A support bot fine-tuned on a policy PDF kept quoting the old refund window months after the policy changed; switching knowledge to RAG fixed it in a day.

questions.promptHtml: Estimate the GPU memory needed to fully fine-tune a 7B model with AdamW. Where does it go?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Back-of-the-envelope memory math is the standard test of whether you understand training versus inference.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Inference only needs the weights: 7B times 2 bytes in bf16 is about 14 GB. Training with AdamW in mixed precision costs roughly 16 bytes per parameter: 2 for bf16 weights, 2 for gradients, 4 for fp32 master weights, and 8 for Adam's two fp32 moments. 7B times 16 is about 112 GB, before activations. So it does not fit one 80 GB card without sharding (ZeRO/FSDP), 8-bit optimizers or offload.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Per-parameter bytes: weights bf16 2 + gradient bf16 2 + master fp32 4 + Adam m fp32 4 + Adam v fp32 4 = 16.

  • 7B: 112 GB. 70B: 1.12 TB.
  • Activations come on top and scale with batch size times sequence length times layers; gradient checkpointing trades roughly 30% extra compute for a large activation saving.
  • Sharding: ZeRO-3/FSDP splits weights, grads and optimizer state across GPUs, so 8 GPUs hold about 14 GB of state each for 7B.
  • PEFT removes gradients and optimizer state for the frozen base: LoRA on 7B keeps 14 GB of weights plus a few hundred MB for adapters and their Adam state.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Training is Python only.

params = 7e9
print(params * 2 / 1e9, "GB inference bf16")           # 14
print(params * 16 / 1e9, "GB full FT with AdamW")      # 112

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Forgetting optimizer state, the biggest single item.
  • Ignoring activations and the KV/attention buffers at long sequence length.
  • Assuming 8-bit weights during training make the optimizer state small too (it does not unless the optimizer is also 8-bit).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How does LoRA change this? → Base needs only weights (14 GB); gradients and Adam state exist only for adapters.
  2. What does gradient checkpointing do? → Recomputes activations in backward instead of storing them: less memory, more compute.
  3. Why master weights in fp32? → bf16 has few mantissa bits; small updates would be rounded away.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "need many GPUs." Senior: breaks down the 16 bytes, adds activations, and names sharding and checkpointing as the levers.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A job OOMed at step 1 on a 80 GB card because the plan counted only weights and gradients; Adam state added 56 GB.

questions.promptHtml: How do you choose LoRA rank, alpha, target modules and learning rate? What happens when each is wrong?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates people who copied a notebook from people who can tune and debug a run.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Rank r sets capacity; 8 to 16 suffices for style/format tasks, 32 to 64 for harder skills, with diminishing returns. Alpha scales the update by alpha over r, so it acts like a step-size multiplier; I commonly use alpha equal to r or 2r and then tune learning rate. Target modules: all attention projections at minimum, adding the MLP projections for more capacity. Learning rate is higher than for full fine-tuning, around 1e-4 to 3e-4 with warmup and cosine decay. I tune by running small sweeps against a real task eval, not training loss.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Rank too low: underfits, validation loss plateaus high; too high: more memory, easier overfitting, little gain.
  • Alpha: update magnitude is (alpha/r) times BA. Doubling alpha at fixed r is similar to raising the learning rate for the adapter. Some setups (rsLoRA) scale by alpha over sqrt(r) so higher ranks stay stable.
  • Targets: attention-only is the original recipe; adding MLP layers (gate/up/down) usually helps harder tasks and is where most parameters are.
  • Dropout 0 to 0.1 on the adapter input as regularization; often 0 for large datasets.
  • LR: 2e-4 is a common LoRA start (versus ~1e-5 for full fine-tuning). Too high gives loss spikes; too low gives flat curves.
  • Epochs: 1 to 3 for typical instruction sets; more risks memorization.

Order of tuning: fix data quality, then LR, then targets, then rank.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Training is Python only.

from peft import LoraConfig
cfg = LoraConfig(r=32, lora_alpha=64, lora_dropout=0.05,
                 target_modules=["q_proj","k_proj","v_proj","o_proj",
                                 "gate_proj","up_proj","down_proj"],
                 task_type="CAUSAL_LM")
# args: learning_rate=2e-4, lr_scheduler_type="cosine", warmup_ratio=0.05, num_train_epochs=2

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Raising rank to fix a data problem.
  • Changing rank and alpha together so you cannot tell which helped.
  • Using the full-fine-tuning learning rate (1e-5), which makes adapters barely move.
  • Judging by train loss only.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why alpha over r? → Keeps the update scale roughly constant when you change r.
  2. Which modules matter most? → Often MLP plus attention; exact winner is task dependent, so test.
  3. Does bigger rank always help? → No; returns diminish and overfitting grows with small data.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "r=16, alpha=32, default." Senior: explains each knob's effect, gives a tuning order, and ties selection to a task eval.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A run at r=8 attention-only stalled at 71% format validity; adding MLP targets (no rank change) reached 96%.

questions.contextHtml:
You LoRA-tune an 8B instruct model on 6,000 support conversations. Training loss goes from 2.1 to 0.35 in 200 steps, which looks great. In testing the model answers correctly but sometimes keeps generating a fake "User:" turn after its answer and never stops, and in the API it ignores the system prompt. The data code is:

def fmt(ex):
    text = f"User: {ex['question']}\nAssistant: {ex['answer']}"
    return tokenizer(text, truncation=True, max_length=512)
# labels = input_ids (loss on every token)

Average conversation is 640 tokens.
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong, and how do you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Train longer" or "lower the learning rate". Misses template, masking and truncation entirely.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which model and exact chat template does serving use? Is an end-of-turn token in the data? How many examples exceed 512 tokens? Is the loss computed on the prompt?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Pull the tuned adapter from traffic and serve the base instruct model while I fix data.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) hand-written template differs from the model's native chat template, so no system role and no end-of-turn token learned; (b) no EOS/end-of-turn in targets, so the model never learns to stop; (c) 512 truncation cuts answers (average 640) so many examples end mid-sentence; (d) loss on the prompt inflates apparent progress (low loss from copying user text).
  4. How I'd verify each: Print tokenizer.apply_chat_template(msgs, tokenize=False) and diff against my string; count examples where the final token is not the end-of-turn token; histogram of lengths; check label mask fraction.
  5. Root cause: Training format differed from inference format, no stop token in targets, truncation, and unmasked prompt loss.
  6. Fix: Use the model's own chat template, append the end-of-turn token to the assistant turn, set prompt labels to -100, raise max length to cover p99 (or drop/split long ones), then retrain.
  7. Prevention: A unit test that renders one example and asserts template match, EOS present, and mask only on assistant tokens; log token-length histogram each run.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not just raise epochs; I would not hand-build the template because it silently drifts from the one used at serving.
msgs = [{"role":"user","content":q},{"role":"assistant","content":a}]
prompt = tokenizer.apply_chat_template(msgs[:-1], tokenize=False, add_generation_prompt=True)
full = tokenizer.apply_chat_template(msgs, tokenize=False)
p_ids = tokenizer(prompt, add_special_tokens=False)["input_ids"]
f_ids = tokenizer(full, add_special_tokens=False)["input_ids"]
labels = [-100]*len(p_ids) + f_ids[len(p_ids):]   # loss only on the assistant turn

Training code is Python only.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why does masking change the loss value? → Prompt tokens are often easy to predict; excluding them gives a harsher, more honest number.
  • What if you pack many examples into one sequence? → Need attention masking or document boundaries so examples do not leak into each other.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A tuned model looped forever in production because the end-of-turn token was stripped by a preprocessing step; the fix was one line, the outage cost a day of token spend.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames hyperparameters.
  • Hire: spots template mismatch and missing EOS.
  • Strong hire: also finds truncation and mask issues, adds a render-and-assert test.

questions.promptHtml: What exactly is QLoRA? Which parts are new compared with LoRA, and what does it cost you?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: QLoRA is how most people fine-tune big models on limited hardware; interviewers want the specific tricks.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: QLoRA is LoRA on top of a base model stored in 4 bits. The base weights are quantized (compressed) to 4-bit NormalFloat (NF4) with double quantization, which also quantizes the scaling constants; the LoRA adapters stay in bf16 and are the only trained parameters; gradients flow through the dequantized weights; paged optimizers spill optimizer state to CPU memory during spikes. This lets a 65 to 70B model train on one 48 to 80 GB GPU. The cost is slower steps from dequantization (often 20 to 40%) and a small quality loss.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Quantization stores each weight in fewer bits. NF4 is a 4-bit data type whose 16 levels fit the roughly normal distribution of pretrained weights, so it loses less than uniform 4-bit. Weights are quantized in small blocks, each with a scale; double quantization compresses those scales too, saving about 0.4 bits per parameter.

Memory for 70B: 70e9 * 0.5 bytes = 35 GB for weights (about 38 to 40 GB with overhead), plus adapters, activations and a small optimizer state. With gradient checkpointing this fits about 48 GB, versus more than 1 TB for full fine-tuning.

Runtime: each forward/backward dequantizes a block to bf16 on the fly, computes, and discards it. The base is never updated, so quantization error is a fixed offset the adapters learn to compensate.

questions.promptHtml: After training a LoRA adapter, do you merge it into the base model or serve it separately? What are the trade-offs, and how does a client call each?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Deployment choices decide latency, cost and flexibility; this is where PEFT meets production.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Merging computes W' = W + (alpha/r)BA once and saves a normal model: zero extra inference cost and compatible with any engine, but you lose swap-ability and need one full copy per variant. Keeping the adapter separate lets one base model serve many adapters chosen per request (multi-LoRA serving in vLLM or S-LoRA), which is far cheaper for many tenants, with a small per-request overhead. One tenant with high traffic: merge. Many tenants or fast iteration: dynamic adapters.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Merge: W' = W + (alpha/r) * B @ A. Latency identical to the base. Storage: full model per variant.
  • Dynamic: base weights stay loaded in GPU memory; adapters (tens of MB) are loaded and applied per request; batching mixes requests for different adapters in one pass. Adapter swap is a cache fill, not a model reload.
  • Caveats: merging into a quantized base needs care (merge into a 16-bit copy); re-evaluate after merge and after any serving quantization.
  • Training is Python only; the client side is language-agnostic because engines like vLLM expose an OpenAI-compatible HTTP API where the adapter appears as a model name.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Collect more data" with no mention of checkpoint choice, epochs or capacity, or "train loss is great, ship it".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the test set disjoint from training (no duplicate tickets)? Was there a validation split? Do eval and training use the same template? What does the best prompted baseline score?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Serve the base model with the best prompt (70%) until a better checkpoint exists.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) overfitting: val loss minimal near epoch 3 then rises, train loss approaches 0; (b) too much capacity for 1.8k examples (r=64, all layers, high LR); (c) duplicate or templated tickets enabling memorization; (d) distribution mismatch between val and test.
  4. How I'd verify each: Plot curves; evaluate saved checkpoints at epochs 2 to 4 on the task metric; run near-duplicate detection (MinHash) between train and test; compare memorized n-gram overlap in outputs.
  5. Root cause: Eight epochs on a small set with high capacity memorized the data; I picked by train loss.
  6. Fix: Early stopping on validation task metric (around epoch 2 to 3), 2 to 3 epochs, r=16, lr 1e-4 to 2e-4, dropout 0.05, dedupe, add more varied data or mix general instruction data.
  7. Prevention: Save checkpoints each epoch, select on the task eval, alert when val loss rises for 2 evals, cap epochs by dataset size.

questions.promptHtml: Why is B initialized to zero and A random, and what would break if both were zero or both random?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests real understanding of the gradient flow, not just formulas.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Delta-W is B times A. If B is zero, delta-W starts at zero, so the model begins exactly as the pretrained base. A must be non-zero random because the gradient to B is proportional to A's output; and B's gradient is non-zero from step 1 so B learns, after which A also gets gradient. If both were zero, both gradients would be zero and nothing would ever train. If both were random, the model would start off-distribution with a noisy delta and early training would be unstable.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Let h = A x (r-dim). Output delta = B h. Gradient wrt B is (dL/dy) h^T, which is non-zero if h is non-zero, which requires A non-zero. Gradient wrt A is B^T (dL/dy) x^T, which is zero while B is zero but becomes non-zero after the first update of B. So training bootstraps in one step.

Parameter count: r(d + k) for adapters versus d*k. With d=k=4096, r=16 the saving is 128x per matrix. Over a model with 224 adapted matrices (32 layers, 7 projections) at d=k=4096 that is on the order of tens of millions of trainable parameters (exact number depends on MLP shapes).

Scaling by alpha/r keeps the update magnitude comparable if you change rank.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Training is Python only.

import torch
d = k = 4096; r = 16
A = torch.randn(r, k) * (1/ r**0.5)    # random (PEFT uses kaiming-uniform; verify in docs)
B = torch.zeros(d, r)
x = torch.randn(k)
assert torch.allclose(B @ (A @ x), torch.zeros(d))   # delta-W x == 0 at step 0

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Initializing both from Gaussian "to be symmetric".
  • Thinking zero init makes B stuck; it is only zero-gradient for A at step 0.
  • Forgetting alpha/r in the merge formula.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What if A is also zero? → Both gradients vanish; no learning.
  2. Parameters per layer for r=32, d=4096, k=11008? → 32 * (4096 + 11008) = 483,328.
  3. What do variants like PiSSA change? → Initialize adapters from the principal singular components of W for faster convergence; verify on your task.

sections.html: "Wait for 8 GPUs" or "rent more GPUs" with no arithmetic, no smaller baseline and no eval plan.

sections.label: Strong answer

  4. How I'd verify each: Weights NF4: 70e9 * 0.5 = 35 GB (about 38 to 40 GB with quantization constants). Adapter plus Adam state at r=16: well under 2 GB.   7. Prevention: Measure tokens/sec early; set a go/no-go gate after 20% of training.

questions.promptHtml: What is catastrophic forgetting in fine-tuning, how do you detect it, and how do you reduce it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tuned models that win the task but lose everything else are a classic production regression.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Catastrophic forgetting means that after training on a narrow dataset, the model gets worse at things it used to do: general reasoning, other languages, safety refusals. I detect it by running a regression suite of general benchmarks and in-house probes before and after. I reduce it by using LoRA with a modest rank, a low learning rate, fewer epochs, mixing 5 to 30% general instruction data into training (replay), and optionally a KL penalty toward the base model.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Gradient updates for the new task move weights that other abilities also depend on. Full fine-tuning at high LR is the most exposed; LoRA limits how far the weights can move because the update is low-rank and the base is intact ("LoRA learns less and forgets less").

Mitigations in order of cost:

  1. Fewer epochs, smaller LR, early stopping.
  2. Lower rank / fewer targets.
  3. Data mixing: include general instruction or replay examples.
  4. Regularization toward base (KL divergence on logits, or weight decay to base).
  5. Merge/average with base weights (scaled adapters, e.g. multiply the adapter by 0.5 to 0.8 at serving).

Detection: fixed panel of benchmarks (reasoning, instruction following, multilingual), safety probes, and the pre-tuning baseline numbers stored with the run.

questions.promptHtml: Validation loss went down. How do you actually decide that a fine-tuned model is better and safe to ship?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Teams ship regressions because loss is not the product metric.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Validation loss only measures next-token prediction on held-out text; it does not measure whether the answer is correct, well-formatted or safe. I compare the tuned model with the prompted base and a strong baseline on a held-out task set using task metrics, check behavioral properties (format validity, refusals, tool-call accuracy, long inputs), run a regression suite for general abilities and safety, review samples with humans or a calibrated LLM judge, and measure cost and latency. Ship only if it wins on the task without regressions.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Layers of evaluation:

  1. Task metrics on a frozen test set never used for checkpoint selection (accuracy, F1, exact match, rubric score).
  2. Behavioral checks: JSON schema validity rate, stop-token behavior, tool-call correctness, length and language handling.
  3. Regression suite: general benchmarks plus in-house probes; compare to pre-tuning numbers.
  4. Safety: red-team prompts, refusal rates; fine-tuning can erode safety.
  5. Human review: sample 50 to 100 outputs; calibrate an LLM judge against humans, and watch judge bias (length, self-preference).
  6. Cost/latency: tokens per answer, throughput on target hardware. Report with confidence intervals: with 200 items a 3-point gap may be noise.

  2. Immediate mitigation: Roll back to the base model or the previous adapter; if it is not possible, add an input/output safety classifier in front.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) benign fine-tuning shifts the model toward compliance and helpfulness, eroding refusals (a known effect); (b) training data had no refusals, so that behavior was not reinforced; (c) high rank/LR moved weights further; (d) persona style makes refusals less likely.

questions.promptHtml: You trained with QLoRA. How do you produce the model you will actually serve, and what can go wrong?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The train-time and serve-time base differ, which is a source of subtle quality loss.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The adapter was trained against a 4-bit quantized base, but the clean way to ship is to load the original 16-bit base, apply the adapter, merge into 16-bit, and then optionally quantize again for serving with AWQ, GPTQ or FP8. Merging directly into 4-bit weights loses precision. After each step, I re-run the eval, because quantization error and merge rounding can change behavior. Alternatively I serve the 16-bit base with the adapter unmerged.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Training saw dequant(NF4(W)) + BA. At serving with a 16-bit base the model computes W + BA. There is a small mismatch because the adapters learned to compensate for 4-bit error; in practice quality is usually close, but must be measured.
  • Merge into 16-bit: W' = W + (alpha/r) BA in bf16/fp16; watch for rounding of small deltas relative to large weights.
  • Post-merge quantization (AWQ/GPTQ/FP8) is a separate error source; calibration data should resemble production inputs.
  • Option: serve with the unmerged adapter on a quantized base (supported in some engines) to match training more closely; verify support and measure.
  • Pipeline discipline: record base revision hash, adapter hash, merge script, quantization config.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Merge is Python only.

import torch
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM

questions.contextHtml: A B2B platform serves 40 customers each with a merged 8B model (16 GB) on dedicated GPUs: 40 GPUs, mostly 5 to 10% utilized, $25k/month. Sales expects 400 customers next year. Each customer's tuned behavior is a LoRA of r=16 (about 80 MB). Latency target p95 2 s. Tests of a single vLLM instance with multi-LoRA show p95 2.4 s at 20 adapters active and adapter cache misses causing occasional 5 s spikes.
questions.promptHtml: Design the serving and rollout plan for 400 tenants.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Buy 400 GPUs" or "load all adapters on every GPU" with no thought about cache, routing or isolation.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Distribution of traffic across tenants (long tail?)? SLA per tenant? Are all adapters the same rank and base? Isolation requirements? Cold-start tolerance?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Keep the 40 existing dedicated tenants as is; migrate low-traffic tenants first.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) spikes come from adapter loading from disk/CPU on cache miss; (b) 2.4 s p95 from mixed-adapter batching overhead or too many concurrent adapters; (c) GPU memory split between KV cache and adapter slots; (d) the red herring: merging is not needed for latency.
  4. How I'd verify each: Metrics on adapter load times and cache hit rate; run load test at skewed traffic (80% from 10% of tenants); vary max adapters per GPU; profile time to first token.
  5. Root cause: Adapter cache sized too small for the active set, and no routing affinity.
  6. Fix: Route by tenant hash to a small pool so each replica sees about 20 to 30 hot adapters; pin top tenants; pre-load adapters at deploy; tune the max-adapter and rank limits; keep adapters on fast local storage; hot tenants with strict SLAs stay merged on dedicated GPUs.
  7. Prevention: Per-tenant metrics, eval per adapter before enabling, versioned adapter registry, canary.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: No merging into 400 full copies (6.4 TB). Isolation: adapters share a base but not a context; validate that request routing cannot cross tenants. Estimated cost: perhaps 8 to 12 GPUs vs 400 (verify with load test).

questions.promptHtml: When does LoRA underperform full fine-tuning, and how do you tell whether you need to escalate?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Seniors need to know the ceiling of the default method and the evidence for leaving it.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: LoRA constrains the update to low rank, so it underperforms when the task needs large, high-rank changes: new languages, big domain shifts like code or biomedical text, and knowledge-heavy continued pretraining. Before escalating I try higher rank, all linear layers as targets, better data and a tuned learning rate (LoRA's best LR is usually about 10x higher than full fine-tuning); if a measured gap remains after those, then full fine-tuning or continued pretraining. For typical instruction and format tasks, LoRA is close to full fine-tuning.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Empirical reports (for example "LoRA Learns Less and Forgets Less") find that LoRA lags full fine-tuning more on harder, data-rich tasks such as code and math continued pretraining, while forgetting less; verify numbers for your model family. Mechanism: the weight changes of full fine-tuning have higher effective rank than small-r adapters can express.

Escalation ladder:

  1. Fix data and prompts/templates.
  2. Add targets (MLP), increase r (32 to 128), tune LR.
  3. Try variants: DoRA, rsLoRA, LoRA+ (different LRs for A and B); verify gains on your own eval.
  4. Continued pretraining on domain text, then SFT.
  5. Full fine-tuning with FSDP/ZeRO and a low LR (~1e-5).

Decision signal: training loss itself stays high and validation plateaus even though data is clean; scaling rank shows continued gains.

  2. What does rank ablation tell you? → If quality keeps rising at each doubling, capacity is the bottleneck.
  3. How about forgetting trade-off? → LoRA forgets less; full fine-tuning may need replay.

questions.contextHtml:
A QLoRA run on a 34B model, lr 5e-4, no warmup, effective batch 8, bf16, 4,000 steps. Log:

step  120  loss 1.18  grad_norm 0.9
step  310  loss 1.05  grad_norm 1.4
step  460  loss 9.84  grad_norm 118.2
step  470  loss nan   grad_norm nan

A restart from step 300 repeats the spike around step 450. GPU utilization looks normal; data loader shuffles with a fixed seed. A colleague suspects bad hardware.
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose and fix.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Restart and hope" or "buy different GPUs" without examining LR, data batch or gradient clipping.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Was gradient clipping on? Was warmup used? Which examples fall in steps 440 to 460? Same behavior on a different node?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Stop the run; keep the last good checkpoint (step 300).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) LR 5e-4 with no warmup and batch 8 is too aggressive for a 34B model; (b) a bad batch (extremely long or malformed example, empty labels producing NaN loss); (c) fp16/bf16 overflow in a specific layer; (d) hardware fault (red herring: deterministic repeat at the same step points to data or LR).
  4. How I'd verify each: Dump example IDs for steps 440 to 460 and inspect; check for sequences with all labels masked (division by zero); rerun with LR 1e-4 and clipping; run the same step on another node; log per-layer grad norms.
  5. Root cause: The deterministic repeat with a fixed seed implicates the data order or LR; here a combination: high LR without warmup plus an outlier batch with an all-masked sample.
  6. Fix: Warmup 5%, lr 1e-4 to 2e-4, gradient clipping at 1.0, filter examples with no assistant tokens, larger effective batch (32 to 64), resume from step 300.
  7. Prevention: NaN guard that skips the step, data validation pass, alerts on grad_norm over 10x moving average.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not simply lower precision or disable the check; gradient clipping slightly slows learning but protects the run. Training is Python only.

questions.promptHtml: Compare prompt tuning, bottleneck adapters, LoRA, continued pretraining and DPO-style preference tuning. When would you pick each?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests breadth and whether you pick the lightest tool that clears the eval.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Prompt/prefix tuning learns a few soft vectors prepended to the input: very light but usually weaker. Bottleneck adapters insert small modules between layers: effective but add inference latency unless fused. LoRA adds mergeable low-rank updates: the best default. Continued pretraining keeps training on raw domain text to absorb vocabulary and knowledge before SFT: expensive, for big domain shifts. DPO, KTO and ORPO use preference data (chosen vs rejected answers) to shape quality and safety after SFT. I go prompt, LoRA SFT, preference tuning if needed, and only then heavier methods.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Soft prompts: trainable embeddings, almost no parameters, works better as models get larger.
  • Adapters: sequential modules, extra layers executed at inference.
  • LoRA: parallel low-rank path, mergeable, zero overhead after merge.
  • Continued pretraining: next-token loss on unlabeled domain text (legal, biomedical, code); needs billions of tokens and care to avoid forgetting.
  • Preference optimization: DPO optimizes the policy directly on pairs without a reward model; KTO needs only good/bad labels; ORPO merges SFT and preference loss. Use when the failure is "style/quality ranking" rather than missing skill.
  • Others: distillation (smaller student from a strong teacher), model merging (TIES, DARE), retriever fine-tuning with (query, positive, hard negative) triples.

  2. Why does DPO use a reference model? → Keeps the policy close to the SFT model via a log-ratio.
  3. Distillation vs LoRA? → Distillation changes model size; LoRA changes behavior at the same size.

questions.contextHtml: A fine-tuned 8B (v1) serves 120 req/s of ticket triage with 91% weekly accuracy. The base vendor releases a new base model; the team trained v2 on it with the same data: offline accuracy 93%, p95 latency 1.1 s vs 0.9 s. Traffic has also drifted: a new product line (7% of tickets) has no training examples and its accuracy is 74% on v1. Last month an adapter silently loaded against the wrong base revision, producing garbled output for 40 minutes.
questions.promptHtml: How do you roll v2 out, and what ongoing operations do you set up?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Switch over after offline eval passes."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is v2 evaluated on the new product line? Can we shadow traffic? What is the rollback time? What labels arrive and how quickly (feedback loop)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add a startup check that adapter metadata base-model hash matches the loaded base; fail closed.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) v2 offline win may not hold on drifted traffic; (b) latency increase is acceptable; (c) the 7% new segment will dominate future errors; (d) the earlier incident is a missing version contract, not a model issue.
  4. How I'd verify each: Shadow v2 on live traffic for a week and compare to v1 and to labels; slice metrics by product line; load test p95 at 120 req/s.
  5. Root cause: Release process lacks version binding, slice-aware evaluation and drift monitoring.
  6. Fix: Canary 1% to 5% to 25% to 100% with automatic rollback on accuracy proxy or latency regressions; v1 stays as fallback for 2 weeks; add labeled examples for the new product line and retrain as v2.1.
  7. Prevention: Registry binding dataset version, config, base hash, adapter and eval report; retraining triggers (new-segment share over 5%, accuracy decay 2 points, 3 months); data retention and deletion process.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: No big-bang switch. More frequent retraining costs money and risks regression; set triggers rather than a calendar. Training is Python only.

questions.contextHtml: Two engineers each ran "the same" LoRA recipe. One reports 84% on the eval, the other 79%. Config files are mostly the same: r=16, lr 2e-4, 2 epochs. Differences found in a day of digging: different dataset versions (a cleanup script ran for one), different transformers versions, no fixed seed, effective batch 32 vs 16, and one used the template from the tokenizer config while the other hand-wrote it. Leadership asks "which number is real and can we trust 84%?"
questions.promptHtml: How do you resolve it and prevent it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Average them" or "the 84% is higher, use it".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the eval set identical and frozen? Which differences are intentional? How noisy is the eval (item count)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Do not publish either number; freeze the eval set and dataset version.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) the template difference (largest likely effect); (b) data cleanup; (c) batch size (effective LR); (d) seed noise; (e) library version, usually small.
  4. How I'd verify each: Run a controlled grid changing one factor at a time with 3 seeds each; compute mean and standard deviation; bootstrap confidence intervals on the eval.
  5. Root cause: Uncontrolled factors and an unfrozen configuration, with no seed variance estimate.
  6. Fix: Pin the recipe: dataset hash, library lockfile, seed, chat template from the tokenizer, effective batch; report mean of 3 seeds with interval.
  7. Prevention: Experiment tracker (W&B/MLflow) that stores config, git commit, data hash and eval report with each checkpoint; CI check that rejects runs without them.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: 3 seeds triple cost; for expensive runs use 1 seed for sweeps and 3 only for the finalist. Training is Python only.
